Number the chain from the double-bonded end: \(\overset{1}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2=\overset{2}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\overset{3}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2-\overset{4}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2-\overset{5}{\text{C}}\equiv\overset{6}{\text{C}}\text{H}\).

The hybridisation of a carbon follows from the number of \(\sigma\)-bonds it forms (equivalently, the number of atoms attached to it):

- \(\text{C}_2\) is one of the two doubly bonded carbons. It is attached to \(\text{C}_1\), \(\text{C}_3\) and one \(\text{H}\) — three \(\sigma\)-bonds — with the remaining \(p\) orbital used for the \(\pi\)-bond of \(\text{C}_1=\text{C}_2\). Three \(\sigma\)-bonds means \(sp^2\) hybridisation.
- \(\text{C}_3\) is a \(-\text{CH}_2-\) group attached to \(\text{C}_2\), \(\text{C}_4\) and two \(\text{H}\) atoms — four \(\sigma\)-bonds and no \(\pi\)-bond — so it is \(sp^3\) hybridised.

The \(\text{C}_2-\text{C}_3\) bond is therefore formed by the overlap of an \(sp^2\) orbital of \(\text{C}_2\) with an \(sp^3\) orbital of \(\text{C}_3\), i.e. an \(sp^2 - sp^3\) pair.

Note that the \(sp\) orbitals in this molecule belong only to the triply bonded \(\text{C}_5\) and \(\text{C}_6\), which are not involved in the \(\text{C}_2-\text{C}_3\) bond at all; and an \(sp^3 - sp^3\) pair would describe the \(\text{C}_3-\text{C}_4\) bond, not this one.

In Lassaigne's test the organic compound is fused with sodium, so nitrogen is converted to sodium cyanide: \(\text{Na} + \text{C} + \text{N} \rightarrow \text{NaCN}\).

The sodium extract is then boiled with ferrous sulphate. The cyanide ions first form the hexacyanoferrate(II) complex,

\(6\,\text{NaCN} + \text{FeSO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Na}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6] + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4\)

This complex is a colourless intermediate, not the coloured species being looked for. On acidification with concentrated sulphuric acid, some \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) is oxidised to \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\), which reacts with the hexacyanoferrate(II) ion to give the blue precipitate:

\(3\,\text{Na}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6] + 4\,\text{Fe}^{3+} \rightarrow \text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]_3 + 12\,\text{Na}^{+}\)

So the Prussian blue colour is due to ferric ferrocyanide, \(\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]_3\).

The formula can be confirmed by charge balance: four \(\text{Fe}^{3+}\) ions give \(+12\), and three \([\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]^{4-}\) ions give \(-12\), so the compound is neutral. By contrast \(\text{Fe}_2[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]\) balances only if the outer iron is \(\text{Fe}^{2+}\) — that is ferrous ferrocyanide, a white precipitate — and \(\text{Fe}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]_4\) cannot be balanced with either oxidation state of iron.

A carbocation is stabilised by the electron-releasing \(+\text{I}\) effect of the alkyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon and, more importantly, by hyperconjugation — the delocalisation of the \(\text{C}-\text{H}\) \(\sigma\)-electrons of the adjacent carbons into the empty \(p\) orbital. Both effects grow with the number of alkyl groups **directly attached** to the charged carbon, so the order of stability is

\(3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > \text{methyl}\)

Classifying each cation by counting the alkyl groups on the carbon bearing the \(+\) charge:

- \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}.\,\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2\) — the charged carbon carries only one alkyl group, so despite the bulky \(tert\)-butyl group it is a **primary** cation, and it has no \(\alpha\)-hydrogens on the quaternary carbon to hyperconjugate with.
- \((\text{CH}_3)_3\overset{+}{\text{C}}\) — three methyl groups on the charged carbon: **tertiary**, with nine \(\alpha\)-hydrogens available for hyperconjugation.
- \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2\) — one alkyl group: **primary**.
- \(\text{CH}_3\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}\,\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) — two alkyl groups: **secondary**.

The only tertiary cation in the set, \((\text{CH}_3)_3\overset{+}{\text{C}}\), is therefore the most stable.

Chromatography is the most recent and the most widely applicable of the purification techniques. It separates the components of a mixture by their differing distribution between a stationary phase and a moving mobile phase, so it works on very small quantities, on mixtures of many components at once, and on non-volatile or thermally unstable substances — and the separated components can then be recovered individually, which is why it serves for isolation, purification and separation alike.

The other techniques are older and each is restricted by a physical property the sample must happen to possess: crystallisation requires a solvent in which the compound and its impurities differ appreciably in solubility, distillation requires the components to be volatile and to differ sufficiently in boiling point, and sublimation applies only to the few solids that pass directly into the vapour phase on heating.

Compare the two sides of the reaction: the iodine of \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I}\) has been replaced by an \(-\text{OH}\) group, the carbon skeleton being unchanged. One group has taken the place of another, so this is a **substitution**, not an addition (nothing is added across a multiple bond — the substrate is saturated) and not an elimination (no small molecule is lost and no \(\pi\)-bond is created; elimination is what aqueous alkali gives only when it is replaced by alcoholic \(\text{KOH}\)).

To name the type of substitution, identify the attacking species. Iodine is more electronegative than carbon, so the \(\text{C}-\text{I}\) bond is polarised as \(\overset{\delta+}{\text{C}}-\overset{\delta-}{\text{I}}\), leaving the carbon electron-deficient. The attacking reagent is the hydroxide ion \(\text{OH}^-\) from aqueous \(\text{KOH}\), which is electron-rich and donates a lone pair to that carbon — the definition of a nucleophile. The iodide leaves as \(\text{I}^-\), taking the bonding pair with it:

\(\text{HO}^- + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{I} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{OH} + \text{I}^-\)

Since the incoming group is a nucleophile, the reaction is a nucleophilic substitution. It could not be an electrophilic substitution, because an electrophile attacks an electron-rich centre, which a saturated alkyl halide does not offer.
